item.title: Spain announces ban on evictions after protests over 87-year-old woman's removal from flat
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwm2qmjgy93do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Spain announces ban on evictions after protests over 87-year-old woman's removal from flat - Published Spain's coalition government has approved new housing measures following protests over the country's housing crisis, sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last week. Ministers met on Tuesday to discuss the proposals, which include a ban on evictions until 2030. Announcing the measures, Health Minister Mónica García said they would bring relief to more than five million people - but opposition politician Míriam Nogueras said the agreement left "small landlords out in the cold". The proposals - which have been presented in the form of two decrees - come into effect immediately, but must be approved by Congress within a month, although the government hopes to hold the vote as soon as this Friday. Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government lacks a majority in parliament and has struggled to get right-leaning parties to approve previous decrees. In April, a decree seeking to roll over rental contracts was blocked by right-leaning parties. García, of the Sumar alliance, said other measures agreed upon on Tuesday included the rolling over of contracts until 2028; stricter regulation of short-term and room rentals; and banning the purchase of housing by investment firms. "It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds," García said. Referencing the protests, she added: "Thanks to the mobilisations and the encampments. Without you, this would not have been possible." But Nogueras, spokeswoman for the centre-right Catalan nationalists of Junts party, said: "We all agreed that evictions - where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros - obviously need to be stopped. "Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property - putting them all in the same basket - is a mistake," she told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE. The minority government, which is made up of the Sánchez's ruling Socialists and junior partner the Sumar alliance, has 30 days from the decrees' publication to reach an agreement in parliament. Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez urged political parties to support the decrees after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal last week. "Congress has the opportunity to tell Maricarmen that her suffering was worth it... and that many people will benefit from her battle", she said. But Valeria Racu, a spokeswoman for the Madrid Tenants' Union, said the battle had "only just begun", and called for more protests across Spain next weekend. "We all have our eyes on the text, on the small print, to make sure this is the Maricarmen decree," added Alicia del Río, another spokeswoman for the organisation. The two decrees approved by the cabinet contain enough to at least suggest that the government has been listening carefully to the demands of the activists who have been protesting in Madrid, Barcelona and elsewhere in recent days. The temporary ban on evictions, the rolling over of rental contracts and the ban on investment firms - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property are all the kinds of policies that have been discussed by housing activists in recent days. Pablo Bustinduy, minister of social rights, described the measures approved by the cabinet as "a first step towards the economic and social transformation of the country". Bustinduy and his Sumar alliance had entered the negotiations with Sánchez's Socialists determined to take a stand on this issue, which is one they feel strongly about. Sumar's tough stance was a major reason why talks between the coalition partners on the decrees went down to the wire ahead of Tuesday's cabinet meeting. While the relatively bold new measures may please many on the left, they have raised the hackles of the Junts, whose support is again likely to be needed to approve them. Junts and other parties on the right tend to be reluctant to intervene in the housing market, particularly if it means tipping the balance of the law in favour of tenants and against landlords, many of who are their natural electorate. The question now is whether the social momentum generated by the Maricarmen Abascal case will override such reservations and manage to ensure this package of measures becomes law. - The hard men removing squatters in Spain - Published26 August 2021 - Taking back Barcelona's apartments - Published12 December 2015 - 'Sometimes I want to cry': Eviction in a pandemic - Published14 December 2020 Ahead of the government's announcement on Tuesday, the lawyer for Abascal, who has become a symbol of Spain's housing crisis, said she would be allowed to return to her home after reaching a deal with the company that owns it on Monday. Abascal, who was admitted to hospital after being forcibly removed from the apartment on a stretcher, was unable to attend the meeting and is yet to sign the deal. Abascal's father first rented the flat in 1956 and she had continued to live in it after her parents died, with a cap on the rent, until investment company Urbagestión bought the property in 2018. It raised the monthly rent to more than her monthly pension, leaving her unable to pay it. Abascal's case is not unique. In the north-eastern city of Zaragoza, another woman's eviction was temporarily suspended on Tuesday, the European Pressphoto Agency reported. Esmeralda Tejero, 51, has lived in a flat in the city for eight years with her 11-year-old daughter, but stopped paying her rent some time ago as she could not afford it on top of her daily living costs, she told Catalan newspaper el Periódico on Monday. Protests calling for housing relief measures broke out last week in Madrid and have spread to other cities including Barcelona, Seville, Malaga and Cadiz. Thousands marched through the capital on Saturday demanding stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents. Hundreds of tents have been set up in the famous public square of Puerta del Sol since. The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction. House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE. The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents. It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively. - Published10 hours ago - Published6 days ago

item.title: 'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck9qr8jy8ynyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail - Published US journalist Evan Gershkovich has said that he knew he was being set up by Russia when he was arrested by FSB agents and accused of being a spy. In an interview with Radio 4's Today programme, Gershkovich spoke about the moment he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in 2023, and detained him. "I'm not interrogated, I'm not tortured… I'm accused of espionage," he said, describing a sense of relief: "They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage - a pawn in a greater game". Gershkovich, now 34, was sentenced to 16 years in prison, but freed 16 months later as part of a high-profile prisoner swap deal. Gershkovich had been living in Russia since 2017, and was the Wall Street Journal's foreign correspondent in Moscow when he was arrested - he is now based in Berlin, Germany. He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false. On the day he was arrested, Gershkovich was in Yekaterinburg - about 1,600km (1,000 miles) east of Moscow - meeting someone who he thought was a source for a story. They were sitting in a half-empty dining hall "and a group of about half-dozen masked men marched in and said 'I think we booked that table'." An odd phrase, Gershkovich said, but on reflection it is clever because it "freezes you in place". The two men stood up and Gershkovich was told he was under arrest by the notorious and powerful FSB, Russia's domestic security service. "It's at that moment that you realise it's something really serious… When it's the FSB, you know it's been planned." What about the man he'd been meeting? Gershkovich saw him disappear into the crowd. Not long after his arrest, the journalist said he realised that the fact he was not being interrogated or tortured - common tactics used by Russia's security service on spies - likely meant that he was being treated more like a commodity, not a true enemy of the state. "I have this odd moment - a sense of relief flooding over me," he said. "I realised they're not treating me like a real spy. They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage, a pawn in a greater game. That means it will take a while, but I won't be here for 12-20 years." That realisation helped him stay "stable and disciplined in prison", but also gave him a unique way of predicting what might happen next - and one guess was a prisoner swap. "I assumed that it would be really loud, that it would cause a global uproar. I mean, it's a foreign correspondent for the Wall Street Journal," he said - and he was right. Media organisations around the world reported on the case, his face was on a billboard in Times Square and then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home. The journalist believed that this was all part of Moscow's plan - to have a high-profile prisoner that it could swap for one of its own - and that was Vadim Krasikov, an assassin who was serving a life sentence in Germany. "They [Moscow] got away with it in the sense that there were no sanctions imposed. And so they played it really smart, if you think about it cynically." Gershkovich was held in Moscow's infamous Lefortovo jail, which has held some of the country's most high-profile inmates over the years, including political prisoners and dissidents. During the Great Terror of Joseph Stalin in the 1930s, torture and execution were commonplace. He described it as a "really isolating experience", in a tiny space. "That wears on you psychologically," Gershkovich said, but added that he was treated ok: "I was allowed to sleep, the food was fine." Pictures of Gershkovich smiling at cameras during his court appearances in Moscow were broadcast around the world - and that was deliberate, he said - a way of showing that he was alright. "I wanted to show people this kind of defiance... We know that this is a fabricated case, and so if this is a game of theatre, let's not let [Moscow] have it play out the way they want it to." But he stressed that not everyone's time in a Russian prison is like his: "Some people... get tortured. They get broken as human beings, deprived of food, of hot water for showers, told that they're never going to see their families again. I was treated completely differently." Gershkovich compared his experience to the case of Ukrainian journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna, who died while in Russian captivity in 2024, aged 27. Months later, when her body was finally returned, it reportedly showed signs of torture and her organs had been removed. Gershkovich knew there was a prisoner swap planned three weeks before it happened - an "excruciating" time, he said, "because now every day is painfully long". When it finally did happen, on 1 August 2024, it was a moment of "pure joy". But then "the joy fades, the adrenaline subsides, and you're faced with the reality of having to return to normal life again." Gershkovich said this period was difficult and sometimes overwhelming. He wasn't sleeping, suffered panic attacks in large crowds and had a short temper because he was trying to hold in his emotions. He has seen therapists who specialise in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and said writing a book on his ordeal also helped. And what about a return to Russia? Gershkovich has a deep history with the country - his parents moved to the US from the Soviet Union in the 1970s. He grew up in a Russian-speaking home, with a Russian name, moved there when he was 25 and made many friends, including his Russian girlfriend. "I would hope to get back one day, but I guess we'll have to see what comes after [Russian President Vladimir] Putin. And it's not completely clear that the next government will be any better." item.title: Israeli settlers attack West Bank village and block Palestinian family's return home
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvlylj41egxgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Israeli settlers attack West Bank village and block Palestinian family's return home - Published More than 100 Israeli settlers have carried out attacks in a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank, stopping a family escorted by the Israeli military from returning to their homes, which had been seized weeks ago by settlers. Two houses belonging to the al-Tubasi family in Jalud, south of Nablus, were set on fire in the raid on Monday night and Israeli security forces were also targeted by settlers. Human rights groups say the events show how Israeli authorities are failing to take effective action against settler violence. "It was extremely terrifying, beyond words. It's hard to imagine the situation," Mahmoud al-Tubasi told the BBC. "My feeling now is that I am happy to have escaped death. I genuinely expected they were going to kill us." Al-Tubasi, 60, his wife Aida, 51, and their 33-year-old son, Wael, had returned to their properties accompanied by Israeli forces after Israel's High Court ruled earlier this month that they must be allowed to go back. The family was forced to leave this summer after weeks of settler harassment and attacks. Extremist settlers had set up an illegal outpost close to Jalud and besieged three houses, including two belonging to the al-Tubasis' sons who are married with young daughters. Al-Tubasi said that he was called at about midnight and told that there was coordination with Israel's military for his family to go back to their houses. He received a message from Israeli officials saying that if he wanted to reclaim his property he had to go immediately with the army and Israeli border police. By torchlight, the family inspected one home. A video shared with the BBC shows that the settlers had already extensively damaged it - smashing holes through doors, tearing out electrical fittings, ripping up tiles, breaking windows and leaving rubbish strewn about. The toilet was smashed and appeared to be full of human waste. A large number of extremist settlers arrived in Jalud after alerts were posted in WhatsApp groups they use to coordinate action, saying that the Palestinian family they had forced out was returning and should be stopped. "As soon as we entered the house, which had already been completely destroyed, settlers started throwing stones at us. The army responded by firing tear gas at them, but there were so many settlers, more than 150, that the army could no longer control them," al-Tubasi told the BBC. The grandfather says that a group of Israeli soldiers protected his family from the settlers who tried to approach them, using pepper spray to force them back. Settlers slashed the tyres of a military van they were put in and then they were transferred to an armoured military vehicle. As the family was being driven away, the settlers set fire to their car and both of their houses. Video shot from a distance shows smoke billowing from them. Al-Tubasi says that the Israeli security forces "essentially formed a barrier, took us out safely and got us away from there. But they did not take any action against the settlers themselves." An Israel Defense Forces (IDF) statement said that "more than 100 Israeli rioters were present in the village, blocking roads, setting tyres on fire, and throwing stones at security forces." The Israeli military said that three police officers were lightly injured and a security forces vehicle was damaged. It described the Tubasi family as victims of "nationalist crime" adding that "due to the violence, the mission to return the family to their home was not completed." The head of the local council in Jalud told reporters that residents had confronted the settlers leading to clashes which even spread to a nearby village, where a Palestinian woman was assaulted by settlers and her house set ablaze. One month ago, Aida al-Tubasi was attacked by masked Israeli settlers and injured along with American journalists who were interviewing her in Jalud. The high court decision, which criticised Israeli authorities for failing to crack down on settler violence, ruled that the family should be safely returned home by 20 September - more than a week ago. The legal ruling was strongly worded describing Israeli settlers' actions as "a completely unacceptable phenomenon that stands in contrast to the basic values and moral principles of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state." Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that he strongly condemned the attacks on security forces, calling on law enforcement, "to prosecute the rioters to the fullest extent of the law." Israeli police said that they had arrested three people suspected of being involved in the attacks. Speaking at the UN General Assembly last week, Netanyahu dismissed international concerns about settler violence. He accused the media of ignoring attacks on Jewish Israelis and covering "a handful of juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, who throw stones, who chop down olive trees, occasionally they light some fires." According to the Israeli human rights group, Yesh Din, fewer than three per cent of police investigations into settler violence over the last two decades have led to a conviction. Ziv Stahl, its executive director, said the lack of effective law enforcement was because, "the violence is part of a systematic government policy aimed at pushing Palestinians out of the area and expanding Israeli control over land in the West Bank". Netanyahu's government has overseen a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank claiming biblical and legal rights to the land. Some ministers have said they aim to "bury the idea" that an independent Palestinian state could be set up in the territory along with East Jerusalem and Gaza. Settlements and outposts are illegal under international law. Levels of settler violence have reached an all-time high this year, according to the United Nations, which says that since 2023, more than 6,500 Palestinians have been displaced due to settler attacks and access restrictions in the occupied West Bank. In the same time period, the UN's Humanitarian Office (OCHA) has logged 6,199 attacks by Israeli settlers causing casualties or damage, external. According to OCHA, at least 82 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank this year and four Israelis have been killed - members of the security forces and civilians. At least 23 Palestinians were killed in the context of settler attacks. Related topics - Published9 September - Published8 September - Published7 September

item.title: More than 400 detained as France student protests escalate
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c862epne7glyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
More than 400 detained as France student protests escalate - Published More than 400 people, mostly minors, were detained in France on Tuesday over student protests at high schools across the country, the French interior minister said. The demonstrations, which began in Paris and have seen teenagers blockade their schools for days, stem from issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages. At least 10 teachers and several students, as well as 48 law enforcement officials, were injured during Tuesday's protests, officials said. According to the education ministry, at least 400 schools were affected. Pictures and videos appeared to show bins being set alight and bus stops damaged by protesters. "We're here to deliver a message," one 16-year-old female student told the AFP news agency. "We're not here to smash everything up for no reason. We're here precisely to say that the education system is completely broken. There are 34 of us in each class, and it's just not feasible. The teachers are overworked." Taking to X, French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said students have the right to protest, but condemned reports of violence as "indefensible". Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told BFMTV 440 people were detained, adding: "We don't have the final tally yet, but I'm told two thirds led to police custody." French media reported that protesters hurled projectiles at police, who responded with batons and tear gas. Speaking to AFP, Ryad Rani, president of Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents students, accused the French government of "repression" and police of using excessive force. When pressed on the police response to the protests, which has been criticised by several French politicians, Nuñez said it had been "carried out in an extremely proportionate manner". Writing on social media on Tuesday evening, education minister Geffray said: "The right to demonstrate is a fundamental freedom that cannot serve as an excuse for such actions. "To legitimise them or, in this context, to call for extending the blockades is to endanger our students as well as public employees. It is irresponsible." The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris. On Monday, France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu warned any escalation in the student protests would be "irresponsible" following the arrest of 164 people. Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers." The continuing student demonstrations on Tuesday coincided with nationwide walkouts by unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions. Nuñez said these protests, with at least 200,000 participants reported, mostly went without incident. - Published1 day ago

item.title: First female prime minister named in Morocco after winning elections
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674kkjllw17o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
First female prime minister named in Morocco after winning elections - Published Fatima Zahra El Mansouri has been named Morocco's first female prime minister, after her centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in last week's parliamentary elections. Her appointment makes her only the second woman to lead a government in the Arab world, after Tunisia's Najla Bouden. She was named by King Mohammed VI, who chose her as prime minister over the country's football chief Fouzi Lekjaa, a top politician from the same party. El Mansouri, 50, has been the mayor of Marrakesh for a number of years and also served as a minister in the previous coalition government. Morocco is a constitutional monarchy but most power remains in the hands of the king. - How Ceuta, football and Israel shaped Morocco's election - Published7 days ago At a victory press conference, prior to her announcement as prime minister, El Mansouri was asked whether the state would need to make changes to accommodate her in Muslim religious ceremonies attended by the king, including Friday and Eid prayers, where men and women pray in separate sections. She did not directly answer the question, instead praising the king as "the biggest advocate for women" in the country. "His Majesty is the holder of wisdom… If I am entrusted with the responsibility of head of government, it will be a great honour," she said. El Mansouri is one of Morocco's most prominent female politicians. A lawyer by training, she studied at Mohammed V University in the capital, Rabat, before continuing her education in France and the US, specialising in business and corporate law. She entered politics after Pam was founded in 2008 and became the first woman to serve as mayor of Marrakesh in 2009. She returned to the post after the 2021 elections. In the past five years, she served as a minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under former Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch. In February 2024, she became the co-ordinator of Pam's leadership coalition. El Mansouri has rejected her portrayal as an "iron woman", telling Pam's magazine in 2021: "I am neither a woman of steel nor iron... I am a free activist." During her political career, El Mansouri has rarely spoken publicly about women's rights or gender inequality, despite ongoing debates in Morocco over issues such as whether polygamy should be banned and whether men and women should have equal inheritance rights. Under Morocco's constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the party that comes first in elections to the House of Representatives. Pam has been led by a collective leadership since February 2024, rather than a single secretary general. After the results were announced last week, El Mansouri said the decision was ultimately up to the king to choose between her and Lekjaa. In the past, the appointment was largely a formality, as most Moroccan parties were led by a single secretary general, making it clear who would be nominated to head the government. With 97 seats, Pam does not have a majority and will need to form a coalition to reach the 198 seats required for an absolute majority in the 395-member parliament. It is not clear which party it will work with as it has fallen out with the National Rally of Independents (RNI), which led the outgoing government in which Pam was a junior partner. The Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) rebounded with 54 seats, from only 13 in the previous election - buoyed by the return of party leader Abdelilah Benkirane, a former prime minister. After the vote, Benkirane said the party would stay in opposition, refusing a partnership with Pam. item.title: Dutch police arrest suspected member of group that claimed FBI hack
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw5ym18znr0ro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Dutch police arrest suspected member of group that claimed FBI hack - Published Dutch police have arrested a suspected member of the ShinyHunters cyber-crime group that claimed to have stolen sensitive information on all FBI bureau staff - around 38,000 people. After the alleged attack last week, the group claimed to have every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address and phone numbers. In a statement, Dutch police said it had arrested a 24-year-old man from Amsterdam on suspicion of being part of the group, which has also claimed other hacks. The suspect was arrested on 15 September, before the alleged FBI attack. He is also suspected of attempted incitement to commit two murders, police said. Police said they seized his devices and found a "large amount of information" on his laptop, including "details about two murders that were to be committed abroad" that they suspect he may have ordered. The suspect has been held since his arrest. Dutch officials have not ruled out further arrests. Stan Duijf, who leads Dutch investigations into cybercrime, said in a statement: "The ShinyHunters group is responsible for a large number of national and international victims. "It is good that we have been able to arrest a suspect in the investigation into this group." Taking to X, FBI director Kash Patel thanked Dutch partners and said: "As we speak, FBI teams are actively working with partners to obtain and execute more leads in the ongoing investigation based on this arrest." Following the arrest, Brett Leatherman, assistant director of FBI Cyber, urged members of the group to hand themselves in "while the choice is still yours". He added: "Other groups believed anonymity or their friends would protect them... but arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk. "The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you, you know how to find us, we know how to find you." ShinyHunters claimed to have breached the FBI's servers on 21 September and began contacting reporters the next day sharing samples and screenshots of the stolen data. The BBC has seen a small portion of the data, which appears to be genuine. ShinyHunters is an international collective of hackers, believed to have originally started in France. It has been behind a number of high-profile breaches including on Rockstar Games in April and a highly disruptive hack on education platform Canvas in May. The group claims to have found a vulnerability in the Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI to breach multiple systems including FBIJOBS, FBI BEAST, which does background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which holds agent's medical records, and FBI BICS, which holds investigation information. In its message on the dark web, the group said it did not hack the FBI system for money. Instead, the cyber-criminals asked the agency to retract an advisory that it issued in May about the gang, saying it was "offended" by its characterisation. The public service announcement, external, which is still up on the FBI's website, described ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims". "They target major companies across tech, finance, and retail, often stealing millions of customer records at once," the advisory said. - Published4 days ago - Published3 days ago - Published16 July - Published27 March

item.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson at defence company supplying Ukraine
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m27l4er4jxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Estonia blames Russia for arson at defence company supplying Ukraine - Published Russia was behind an arson attack on an Estonian defence company in the capital Tallinn last month, authorities say. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the attack on Milrem Robotics - which supplies Ukraine with unmanned military vehicles - was ordered by Russian special services, but gave no details. Moscow has been accused of launching sabotage attacks in a number of Nato countries that have been helping Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022. Russia denies such allegations and has been quick to reject the Estonian accusation, too. But EU countries have rushed to Estonia's support, adding such attacks will not deter them from helping Ukraine. The attack on Milrem Robotics occurred on the night of 14-15 August. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that, based on information collected by the country's Internal Security Service, "we can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation". Security service chief Margo Palloson told broadcaster ERR that Russia was "constantly planning, looking for opportunities, trying to find people who would carry out attacks", but that last month's arson attack was its first successful attack this year. The foreign minister said the perpetrators had been arrested and Palloson said they were Latvians who had been living in Russia and taken part in previous attacks. Three suspects were arrested in Latvia and extradited to Estonia earlier this month. Margus Tsahkna said that "this act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine". French President Emmanuel Macron responded to Estonia's assessment, saying "the multiplication of these hostile acts represents a dangerous escalation by Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end". He mentioned the incident at Leipzig airport in Germany in August, in which an explosive-laden drone was found near Ukrainian cargo planes. "Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Macron added. An EU spokesman said the 27-member bloc would not cease supporting Ukraine. Nato chief Mark Rutte urged European governments to stay calm and continue supporting Ukraine. "Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine," Rutte said. In August alone, Russia was either accused or suspected of the Leipzig airport attack in Germany, a major fire at a warehouse of a defence firm in Bulgaria, a large explosion at a munitions factory outside Rome in Italy, an attempted arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer in Slovakia, and two suspicious fires in Poland - the latest in a country which has reported several such attacks. Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms that tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. Estonia's internal security service, known as Kapo, said Russia was continuing to look for further opportunities for either sabotage or other hostile acts. "Individuals recruited for such operations may be misled or manipulated and may be given false or fabricated justifications for their actions in an effort to conceal the involvement of the Russian state," Kapo head Margo Palloson said, external. Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. It accuses Nato countries of seeking to destabilise Russia. On Monday, it repeated a threat to use nuclear weapons - on this occasion "to defend its territory should Nato countries attempt to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of our country". Kaliningrad - located between Poland and Lithuania on the Baltic Sea - is strategically important to Moscow because it houses the Russian Baltic Fleet and is one of Russia's only ice-free European ports. It is not immediately clear what prompted the Russian threat, which was swiftly condemned by the Euro-Atlantic alliance. "Nato is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia," Nato spokeswoman Allison Hart said. "We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric." Related topics - Published2 September

item.title: Eiffel Tower chief to quit after female staff replaced by men during religious visit
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crn8e069v7p7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Eiffel Tower chief to quit after female staff replaced by men during religious visit - Published The chief executive of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower will step down after a backlash over female staff being replaced by male colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group. Patrick Branco Ruivo, who has been director general of the Paris landmark since 2018, will leave his job at the end of the year, the company SETE said in a statement. It said an internal investigation found that "operational flaws and shortcomings" in organising the visit led to the "unacceptable" removal of female staff. They were replaced by male colleagues as a delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the Eiffel Tower earlier this month. BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances. At the time, SETE said the Hindu delegation had requested that the visit be organised so as to limit "interactions with women" and said that "these conditions should not have been accepted". A staff union representative said "women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated". Staff at the monument said female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present". The visit led to the closure of the tower as staff went on strike to show their outrage and politicians condemned the incident. Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said after the visit: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors." The Socialist mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Gregoire, called it an "absurd, unjust and unacceptable decision" and ordered two separate investigations. SETE chair Ariel Weil said on Tuesday that he had requested measures and training programmes promoting gender equality to be implemented. "The coming months will allow us to prepare for the leadership transition under the best possible conditions," he said. BAPS apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused" earlier this month, adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service". On its website, the group describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values. It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney. It draws its beliefs from the teachings of Lord Swaminarayan, a late 18th-Century celibate ascetic who is regarded by his followers as an incarnation of Vishnu, the revered Hindu god of preservation. BAPS says the segregation of men and women was introduced for the benefit of women, but critics say 18th-Century beliefs have no place in today's world, and keeping women out in the name of religious practices is discriminatory.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy appears in court as her lawyer pushes for murder case dismissal
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8046wd93l44o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Lindsay Clancy appears in court as her lawyer pushes for murder case dismissal - Published Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of murdering her three children, has appeared in court for the first time since her murder trial fell apart earlier this month. Her defence team on Tuesday argued the judge should dismiss her case but prosecutors said the state had "met its burden" in proving her guilt. Clancy, 36, does not deny killing her three children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional. It is still not clear if she will face a retrial. The request to dismiss the case is among those that will be discussed at a hearing on 2 November, Judge William Sullivan said. One of the motions addressed on Tuesday was from Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, who asked for her to be found not guilty under Rule 25 - a Massachusetts motion that states a defendant should be found not guilty if prosecutors do not argue their case effectively. Reddington also brought a new defence forward arguing there was not enough evidence to prove Clancy killed her children. "This entire case is based on speculation," he said. It was a change of argument from the defence lawyer, who during the trial focused on Clancy's mental health - urging the jury to find her not criminally responsible because of it. Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham called Reddington's argument "laughable". She said state prosecutors had presented numerous pieces of evidence showing Clancy was in a healthy mental state at the time of the murders during the trial. "The Commonwealth met its burden," Buckingham said. She argued Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months, in their Massachusetts home. Judge Sullivan pushed back when both Reddington and Buckingham refused to agree to his suggestion that they might agree to a possible retrial date now ahead of the hearing, saying he wanted to "get this thing moving". He asked both sides to be prepared to discuss possible trial dates at the November hearing. Reddington said he would be unable to go to trial until at least June if the case is retried. District Attorney Timothy Cruz told reporters outside after court that prosecutors have not yet decided if they are going to retry Clancy on murder charges. "We're doing our due diligence, we're going to continue doing that," he said. "We're going to do what we can for the children. That's what this case is about." Following a week of deliberations earlier this month, a Massachusetts jury told Sullivan they could not reach a verdict because of a lone holdout juror and a mistrial was declared on 4 September. item.title: Nigerian dances non-stop for seven days in world record bid
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8r6z2gjzd1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Nigerian dances non-stop for seven days in world record bid - Published A Nigerian dancer has completed a 168-hour dance marathon in Lagos in a bid to set a new world record. Benjamin Daniel, known as "Ben Dancer", aimed to dance for seven days to break the Guinness World Records title for the longest dance marathon by an individual. Cheered on by friends and supporters at Lagos's Freedom Park, the 33-year-old reached his target time at around 03:00 local time but continued dancing for another nine hours until midday, his team says. The physically exhausted dancer has now gone to hospital for a medical check-up. Guinness World Records has confirmed to the BBC that it has received Daniel's application for the title. The current record stands at 127 hours. "Benjamin's application is active and we now eagerly await submission of his evidence, which will then go through our official review and verification process before any record can be confirmed," a spokesperson for Guinness World Records said in the statement. His team said they were "elated" and emotional after watching him complete the challenge, which has been live streamed on social media. Young people gathered in recent days to cheer him on at Freedom Park in Lagos, filming his every move and dancing along from behind the barriers. "It's a beautiful moment. Seeing how far he has come and witnessing him achieve this feat made me incredibly proud and grateful to God," Uche Anumudu, one of those watching, told the BBC. The current record was set by Indian dancer Srushti Sudhir Jagtap in 2023, when she was 16. Her performance focused mainly on kathak, one of India's major classical dance forms. Ben Dancer, who has been dancing professionally for 18 years and began his attempt last Tuesday, drew on Nigeria's rich dance traditions as well as its fast-changing internet culture. Afrobeats was a constant presence during his performance, alongside genres including fuji, jazz and zouk. At times, he swapped his dance clothes for traditional Nigerian outfits, including the flowing agbada and dashiki. Nigeria has more than 250 ethnic groups, with a wide range of cultural traditions. Ben Dancer's team says the performance was intended to reflect that diversity, rather than simply test his physical endurance. He underwent intensive fitness training before the attempt, changing his diet and focusing on carbohydrates and cardiovascular conditioning. During the danceathon, he ate lightly and drank fluids while taking the permitted five minutes of rest for every continuous hour of activity. He chose to dance for several hours at a time before taking an accumulated rest and a medical team was present. The scene around him became something of a street party and videos from the event went viral across social media platforms, drawing more people to the venue. Moronumubo Akodu, who repeatedly visited to support Ben Dancer throughout the week, said she was impressed by his determination but worried about the physical toll. "It is actually insane, but I am so proud of him," she told the BBC. Emmanuel Ulelu, who visited the performance twice, said he noticed a striking change in the dancer's energy. "On day two, you could see the stress," he said. "Even after just three hours of dancing at the location myself, I wondered how he would keep going." But when he returned 16 hours into day five, he said Ben Dancer appeared more energetic than before. "It reminded me that we're capable of doing unbelievable things when how badly we want something matches and surpasses the difficulty of achieving it," he said. Nigeria has also developed a strong relationship with Guinness World Records, particularly in entertainment. In 2023, Nigerian chef Hilda Baci cooked continuously for 93 hours and 11 minutes in Lagos, which Guinness officially recognised as a new record. Her achievement sparked a surge of interest in record attempts in Nigeria, even though others have since surpassed her. Guinness says it received more than 1,500 new applications from the country within two months of her cook-a-thon, including events such as reading, singing, and crocheting. "It's been brilliant to see such strong enthusiasm for record breaking across Nigeria in recent years," a Guinness spokesperson told the BBC. item.title: US prosecutors reopen case of alleged gang rape at Cornell University
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5wyzrm0n74ro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US prosecutors reopen case of alleged gang rape at Cornell University - Published New York state prosecutors said they will reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024. The woman filed a civil lawsuit on 16 September alleging she was drugged and raped by multiple people at a fraternity house at the university. "Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means possible" through a grand jury, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said Monday. Cornell University said that while it supported the case being brought before a grand jury, "any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false". The woman, referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges in her lawsuit that on the night of 19 October 2024, seven men from Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity chapter allegedly assaulted her in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine. Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and was incapable of providing consent. She said she reported the incident to Cornell University Police on 8 November 2024. The lawsuit also contains an image purported to be from a Snapchat fraternity group chat, in which a participant alerted other members, in vulgar terms, to the potential for a sexual encounter with Jane Doe. Van Houten said on Monday that at the time of the assault two years ago, his office concluded that evidence from her statement to authorities did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges. He said he reached out to Jane Doe and her lawyers for more information as he prepared to bring the case to a grand jury. In an interview with ABC News, Van Houten said the Snapchat messages were "crude and vulgar" but "did not have any relevance to the issue of whether Jane Doe consented to what was happening". "The grand jury will consider that as part of the overall picture," he said. In the US legal system, prosecutors convene grand juries to weigh evidence and testimony and eventually vote on whether they merit criminal charges. In his statement, Van Houten included a summary of what Jane Doe told the Cornell University Police Department in 2024 after the alleged attack. He noted the statement differed from the allegations laid out in the lawsuit. "Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped," Van Houten said in a statement on Monday. "On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual." Van Houten added that Jane Doe's lawyers had never been in touch with him to say her original statement was inaccurate or to ask him to reconsider his decision not to bring charges. He later acknowledged "the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them". The BBC has contacted Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. In a statement on Monday obtained by CBS, the BBC's US partner, he said: "In the days following the assault, [Jane Doe] was traumatised, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self-preservation mode." Giuffra said Jane Doe never spoke to anyone other than the officer who took her initial complaint, adding: "I would have expected at the very least that she would have been interviewed several times and evidence collected by law enforcement and a case developed. This is the normal sequence for serious crime investigations." "The defensive posture I have gleaned from the DA's statements leads me to believe that they recognise that there were failures and they are trying to excuse them," he said. Jane Doe also alleged in her civil lawsuit that Cornell did not protect her nor adequately punish the men involved, alleging they were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays". Jane Doe suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the incident and the university's handling, the suit states, adding that news of the incident quickly circulated through the school. An initial court hearing to consider the civil case is scheduled for 23 October in Manhattan. In November 2024, Cornell University issued a public statement regarding the "serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house", saying its campus police department was investigating and that it had suspended the local chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, as well as "a number of students." Cornell also said it had opened an internal investigation as well as a civil rights inquiry under the Title IX law - which bars sex discrimination in schools that receive funding from the federal government, including most universities. The Xi chapter of Chi Phi fraternity remains barred from its campus, Cornell said. On Monday, the university disputed Jane Doe's allegation that it did not adequately investigate or punish the alleged perpetrators. The university said in a statement that the matter was referred to a "panel of trained faculty and staff" that issued "a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell". "None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement," Cornell said. Jeremy Saland, an attorney for one of the men named in the lawsuit, denied the allegations. Saland acknowledged his client "responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat", but "did nothing else." Saland said his client "was involved in no sexual activity nor touched the plaintiff in any way and ingested no ketamine". The case has received national attention following Doe's lawsuit and the announcement the case would be reopened. Several celebrities, including actress Florence Pugh, and US lawmaker Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have spoken out about it. CBS News New York, external has since published excerpts of addtional text messages reportedly exchanged between one of the defendants and a woman who appears to be the person who has made the allegations. The messages were reportedly sent two days after the alleged assault. In one of the messages, screenshots of which were obtained by CBS, one of the men appears to be apologising for "how things went down". He said his memory was "kinda fuzzy", and that he and another man felt bad for being too intoxicated to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand". The woman in the text chain replied saying her memory was "super clouded too" and that they were all intoxicated. She also wrote that "non(e) of the sexual stuff was illegal", that she liked being with him and another man. She suggested that they smoke together again but leave out "the extra 5 billion men and ketamine". Jane Doe's attorney Thomas Giuffra told CBS News that he understood the messages were presented during Cornell's Title IX proceedings and that he believed the panel recognised Doe was in denial when they were sent. The defendant's expulsion suggested to him that the university did not consider the messages to be significant, Giuffra said. There is a mix of outrage and shock on campus, along with "a humungous wave of solidarity" from people across the US, Sophia Dasser, editor-in-chief of the student newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun, told the BBC. The newspaper's editorial board published the names of the men named in the lawsuit and called for an independent, third-party review of the reporting and resolution processes. "Much of the frustration, in my opinion, does stem from how little students really were told over the last two years regarding this case and how opaque the Title IX process is," Dasser said. She noted that other universities publicise anonymous outcome, sanction and process results of sexual assaults on campus, but Cornell University does not. "So all we ask is really, truly transparency to the student body, especially the student body in which the university is responsible for keeping safe," she said. The mayor of Ithaca, New York, where Cornell is located, has called for a moratorium on all student event and special event permits. The pause is in place until the university "conducts an accounting of its protocols to prevent and prosecute crimes of sexual violence". The Ivy League institution on Monday said that a task force on campus sexual assault was formed in 2025 and has made recommendations that have either been implemented or are in development. A 2025 school survey, external found that 35% of undergraduate women and 8% of undergraduate men have reported experiencing sexual assault during their time at Cornell, the report said. The report said that despite a long history of actions to address sexual assault, rates of sexual assault "remain persistently high". If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide., external A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

item.title: Man charged over AI image of crocodile in Singapore reservoir
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6grveg7d9zro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Man charged over AI image of crocodile in Singapore reservoir - Published Police in Singapore have charged a man who is accused of posting an AI-generated image of a saltwater crocodile in a popular reservoir. Ye Lin was charged with communicating a false message and obstructing the course of justice for allegedly deleting the picture and the application he used. The fake image caused public concern, authorities allege. The national water agency suspended its work at the city-state's largest reservoir for two days last month after receiving information that a crocodile had been spotted. Ye Lin, who is from Myanmar, told the court through an interpreter that he intended to plead guilty, according to local media reports. The national water agency said it was alerted to a crocodile sighting in Pandan Reservoir on 20 August. Agency officials and national parks staff conducted search and capture operations in the area. The Singapore Rowing Association and Singapore Canoe Federation were told the suspend their activities. But the following day, the water agency confirmed that the crocodile image was fake and reported it to the police. The case will return to court in November and Ye Lin could face a prison sentence and a large fine if he is found guilty. In Singapore, sending a false message is punishable by up to three years in prison, a fine of up to S$10,000 (about US$7,800; £5,900), or both. Obstructing justice carries up to seven years in prison, a fine, or both. Police allege that Ye Lin created the photo of the crocodile using artificial intelligence before sending it to a colleague. "The man subsequently deleted the image and the related application in an attempt to conceal his actions," the police statement said. It is not clear how the national water agency was notified of the false photo that Ye Lin sent to his colleague.

item.title: Former American Idol contestant and pastor found guilty of murdering wife
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5rm9gv7n07xo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Former American Idol contestant and pastor found guilty of murdering wife - Published A former Ohio music pastor who once appeared on the TV talent competition American Idol has been found guilty of murdering his wife. Caleb Flynn, 40, fatally shot Ashley Flynn twice in the back of the head while she slept at their Ohio home on 16 February this year, then tried to claim that intruders had shot her. Flynn wept in court as the jury delivered its verdict after deliberating for less than three hours. He also was found guilty of the other eight charges against him, which included aggravated murder and tampering with evidence. He faces life in prison without parole. Closing arguments ended on Tuesday in Flynn's trial after eight days of testimony, which included a song played in court that prosecutors say he wrote and dedicated to the woman with whom he was having an affair. Throughout the trial, the prosecution presented evidence including police body camera footage, and activity on Flynn's iPhone and Apple Watch around the time of the murder, which took place in Tipp City, a suburb of Dayton. They also called dozens of witnesses, including his former mistress Alleigha Botner, whom he met while she was an intern at his church. Some of their 100,000 exchanged text messages were read aloud in court. The defence called no witnesses. "I was up until 4am last night crying, literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail," Flynn wrote in a message to Botner, 24, in August 2025. In another message, he wrote: "I just want her dead and gone." Testifying in court, Botner said she now hates Flynn "because I believe that he murdered his wife". During closing arguments on Tuesday, prosecuting attorney Paul Watkins leaned heavily into Flynn's text exchanges, which he said demonstrated the defendant's "hatred" for his wife. He described Flynn as being afraid to lose custody of his daughters in a divorce, as well as his job with his wife's family business and his job at the church. An emotional Flynn was seen in court at times sniffling and wiping tears from his eyes. Watkins also said that when police arrived at the family home in the early hours on 16 February, Flynn told police he had been in his daughters' bedroom when he heard gunfire. Flynn said he found his 37-year-old wife dead in the bedroom, after noticing the garage side door was open. Watkins said Flynn later told investigators he had not been to the garage, contradicting his earlier statement. Flynn's defence lawyer Patrick Mulligan, meanwhile, told the court there was no concrete evidence, saying: "Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn't solve the case." Mulligan said the issue was not whether Flynn was a good husband to his wife, a schoolteacher and volleyball coach, and that evidence of infidelity was not evidence of murder. "They can't find the gun, therefore they blame it on him?" Mulligan questioned, referring to the charge of tampering with evidence that Flynn also faced. Flynn's gun, which had been kept in the console of his truck, has been missing since investigators arrived at the scene and found the truck's centre console open. Earlier in the trial, Botner took the stand as a witness for two days, offering testimony about her nearly 18-month relationship with Flynn. In addition to reading some of their text exchanges, she also explained the lyrics line by line from an AI-generated song. Video of the jury's reaction to the song, including what looked like laughter, went viral. Prosecutors also called Joseph Wilhelm, a special agent from Ohio's Bureau of Criminal Investigations, as a witness. He said multiple apps were uninstalled from Flynn's phone before his wife's death, including Instagram and an AI-music generating app. The music-generating app, Wilhelm said, "related to his relationship with Alleigha Botner". Flynn appeared in 2013 on the 12th series of American Idol, and sang before judges Mariah Carey, Nicki Minaj and Randy Jackson. He was featured in televised auditions, and was given a "golden ticket" to go to Hollywood, but he never reached the main competition. "Music is all I know, it's what I live to do and I love to sing, so that's why I auditioned," he said in videos shown on the programme. "Maybe my wife kinda nudged me a little, too." He is due to be sentenced on 5 October.

item.title: French hard-right leader accuses opponents of 'total war' after claims of antisemitism
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn45k85gj34o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
French hard-right leader accuses opponents of 'total war' after claims of antisemitism - Published The president of France's hard-right National Rally (RN), Jordan Bardella, has said he will sue for libel after a report published antisemitic comments that it alleged he had made as a young activist. The Mediapart website released what it said was the result of "several months" of investigation into "dozens of written conversations" Bardella allegedly had in 2013. With seven months to go before France's presidential elections, Bardella condemned "the beginnings of a total war" aimed at destabilising his party, and RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said she had total confidence in him. The alleged remarks included blatantly antisemitic tropes, and Bardella said they were an attempt to destroy his political career. Mediapart did not produce screen-grabs of any of the alleged remarks. It said it had "independently authenticated" the conversations, which came from "a bigger documentary base corroborated by witness statements". But Bardella, 31 – who is a likely prime minister if Le Pen wins the presidential election – said the allegations were a fabrication aimed at derailing the RN's increasingly confident bid for power. "Everything is going to be done to destabilise the campaign," he told CNews television on Monday night. "Either Mediapart is running this operation itself, or it is being manipulated by interested parties. "Of course I have instructed my lawyer to sue for libel." Le Pen said the alleged remarks "seem so weird that they can only be a forgery – one of those dirty tricks for which Mediapart appears to hold the secret". Among the statements that Mediapart alleges Bardella made when he was 17 or 18 are: "All the banks are owned by Jews"; "The Jew has to dominate other people, crush them and rob them"; and "What they want is a new world order dominated by Israel, with of course Jerusalem as its capital." Mediapart is an avowedly leftwing website which has exposed a number of scandals over the years, though its targets have been politicians of all stripes. The French hard right is riding higher than ever in pre-election polls, with the latest this week, from Toluna-Harris, showing Le Pen a clear victor over whatever rival she faces in the crucial second round in May. According to the survey, Le Pen would pick up 35-36% of the vote in the multi-candidate first round. Her likely opponent in the two-way run-off would be Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the radical left who she would eradicate with 69% of the vote. But in a stark warning for the political establishment, the poll showed that she would also easily beat the most popular centrist candidate Edouard Philippe, with a score of 57%. On Sunday the RN received another boost when results of a partial election for the upper house of parliament, the Senate, produced for the first time enough seats for the party to form an official group. Under Marine Le Pen, daughter of the historic party founder Jean-Marie Le Pen, the RN has made huge efforts to distance itself from the French far-right's antisemitic roots. Last year Bardella was the first senior figure from the party to be invited to Israel, for a conference on antisemitism. Today the party regards militant Islam as a pre-eminent threat – a position it shares with many Jews. The RN even styles itself as a "shield for the Jewish community". The alleged comments from Bardella throw back to a current of far-right thinking that Mediapart says has never been eradicated but only covered up in the new-look party. Leftwing politicians called on Bardella to resign, and the head of the Jewish umbrella organisation Crif, Yonathan Arfi, said the alleged comments "were an illustration of the limits of the RN's clean-up act". But RN deputy Jean-Philippe Tanguy said the source of the allegations was disaffected members of the party who had been expelled years ago because of their antisemitic ideas. "From what I know, it is the antisemitic rabble that were so bravely purged by Marine Le Pen. At the start of the 2010s, they were numerous and well-organised, but they were defeated. These people have always had it in for us." Related topics - Published4 September - Published11 July

item.title: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwly5lmvy38qo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI - Published US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival. Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern. Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November. The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents. During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US was "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and did not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors. "If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China." Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remained steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology. "Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way". Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hindered AI governance. At a later White House lunch with representatives of government agencies and technology companies - including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta - Trump said among those present, there was "a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation". Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Trump said that the technology leaders had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from the potential hazards of AI. A "Super Intelligence Czar" would likely be named in the coming days, Trump added. The president signed an executive order, external on Tuesday afternoon that will formally change the name of AI to "Super Intelligence" in government documents. Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place. A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity. A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused. The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats". - Published1 day ago - Published16 September - Published7 days ago

========================================
Argentina threatens legal action against UK over Falkland Islands oil exploration - Published Argentina's president has threatened to launch a legal challenge against the British government unless it halts oil exploration work off the coast of the Falkland Islands. In a social media post, President Javier Milei set a two-week deadline for the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies, to be scrapped. The companies insist they have valid licences issued by Britain. The comments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the archipelago, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982. Milei said that if the two-week deadline was not met, he had "instructed the Foreign Ministry and legal teams to initiate international arbitration" against the UK over what he called "the illegal plundering of our resources through the Sea Lion Project". He continued to warn the UK that if the "illegitimate exploitation" of the region didn't end within two weeks, Argentina would take the matter before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. The International Tribunal is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea. The move comes soon after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats". Since then, the UK Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said that Argentina "lacks the ability" to seize the Falklands by force. Milei had previously said the Sea Lion oilfield was a "clear and present danger". The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil. Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years. Both companies have in the past stressed that Sea Lion holds valid licences from the Falkland Islands. In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against. Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them. The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel. Related topics - Published8 September - Published18 September

item.title: Hurricane Polo makes landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8d3z5y7958o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Hurricane Polo makes landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast - Published Hurricane Polo has made landfall along the northern Pacific coast of Mexico, lashing the state of Baja California Sur with life-threatening winds and heavy rain that has already flooded some coastal areas. Mexican officials said Polo moved ashore just south of the surfing and fishing village of Las Barrancas bringing maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 km/h). Polo is moving northeast and on the forecast track, its core is predicted to continue passing over Baja California Sur before moving inland over the southern part of the Mexican state of Sonora later on Tuesday. Residents in threatened areas have been encouraged to seek shelter. Shopkeeper María Palomino, 57, spent the night at a high school which has been turned into a temporary shelter. "If something happens, it's better to come to the shelter," she told AFP news agency. A whale-watching and fishing guide who was boarding up the facade of his home told AFP the storm was "coming with full force". The US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) said that while Polo was expected to weaken as it moved over the Baja California peninsula, it was forecast to still be at hurricane strength when it makes its second landfall in mainland Mexico. Meteorologists said Polo could dump between 6 and 12 inches (150-300mm) of rain across parts of Baja California Sur, which they warned could produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain. The NHC said a storm surge was also expected to produce significant coastal flooding in areas of onshore winds. "Near the coast, the surge will be accompanied by large and destructive waves," it said in an update. Even before Polo made landfall, residents said there were power cuts in Baja California Sur. US media reported some flooding in the fishing town of Puerto San Carlos and the Associated Press said waves crested sea barriers in the area, where many residents had been evacuated due to the threat. Meteorologists said dangerous surf and rip currents were likely to continue along portions of the north-western coast of Mexico and Baja California for the next day or so. The south of the peninsula is popular with tourists and acts as a base for surfers, sport fishers, and whale watchers. In Cabo San Lucas, famous for its natural rock arch, authorities had restricted access to the beaches on Monday. Polo has been slowly moving towards Mexico's coast line for days. Meteorologists said it was being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, which has led to a more active hurricane season in Pacific waters. As Polo moves north-east, it is expected to also affect the US, sending a surge of tropical moisture northwards for the next few days leading to excessive rainfall and flash flooding. Rain has already been falling across Arizona and California but the remains of Polo and another hurricane - named Odalys - will become absorbed into that weather system, boosting the amount of rainfall. These fronts will push eastwards across the southern plains. Some spots could see as much as 6 or 7 inches of rainfall by Thursday. States affected include Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah into Tuesday. Related topics - Published7 days ago - Published6 days ago

item.title: US ban on Canadian alcohol and dairy takes effect as trade war drags on
